About Athenaeum

English studies, calmly organised

Athenaeum is an English studies platform built around clear explanation and steady practice. It brings grammar, sentence structure, vocabulary and the history of the language together in one academic workspace.

Your lessons, notes, quiz results and progress are saved to your account, so you can sign in on any device and carry on where you stopped.

📚 Structured lessonsWork through English studies at your own pace with lessons, notes and progress tracking.
🏆 Quiz ArenaTest yourself, take on challenges and climb the leaderboard.
✏️ Reed–Kellogg Sentence DiagramSee how sentences are built by diagramming them step by step.
🧩 Sentence Structure LabPractise clauses and structure with levels that build to a certificate.
📜 History of EnglishFollow the language from Old English to the World Englishes of today.

An account lets Athenaeum save your progress, notes and quiz results and sync them across your devices.

What do I need to use it?

A current web browser and an internet connection for signing in and syncing.

X-bar Diagram Exercise

Build phrase structure by identifying the specifier, head, complement, and adjunct. This is a separate practice activity; your existing sentence-diagramming work is unchanged.

Before you begin: What is an X-bar diagram?

Purpose: X-bar theory shows the internal structure of a phrase and how its words are organized around a central head.

How it works: Every phrase has a head (the main noun, verb, adjective, or preposition). The head projects to an X′ level; a complement completes the head's meaning, an adjunct adds optional detail, and a specifier appears at the phrase edge. The full phrase is XP.

How to do it: (1) Identify the phrase type and its head. (2) Find any required complement. (3) Add optional modifiers as adjuncts. (4) Check for a specifier. (5) Build upward from X to X′ to XP. Not every phrase contains all three extra parts.

Example: “the student of linguistics” — the head is student (N); “of linguistics” is its complement; “the” is the specifier.

Identify heads and basic complements.

the student of linguistics

Traditional / Immediate Constituent (IC) Phrase Structure Trees

Choose the tree that correctly groups the sentence into immediate constituents. Each answer includes feedback explaining why the selected structure is correct or incorrect.

Before you begin: What are IC phrase-structure trees?

Purpose: Immediate Constituent (IC) analysis shows how a sentence is divided into meaningful grammatical groups, or constituents.

How it works: A sentence (S) is commonly divided into a noun phrase (NP) and a verb phrase (VP). Each phrase can be divided into smaller constituents, such as determiner (Det) + noun (N), or verb (V) + object NP. The branches show which words belong together.

How to do it: (1) Find the main verb. (2) Identify the subject phrase. (3) Identify the predicate/VP. (4) Divide each phrase into its immediate parts. (5) Keep words together when they form one grammatical unit; do not group words just because they are adjacent.

Example: “The child laughed” → S branches into NP (“The child”) and VP (“laughed”).

Question 1 of 10

Identify the immediate constituents.

Which tree is correct?

Dependency Tree Lab

Practise identifying heads and grammatical relations in dependency trees.

Before you begin: What is a dependency tree?

Purpose: A dependency tree shows how words in a sentence depend on other words to form grammatical relationships.

How it works: Each sentence has one root (usually its main predicate). Other words attach directly or indirectly to a head. The links are labelled with grammatical relations such as nsubj (nominal subject), obj (object), det (determiner), and amod (adjectival modifier).

How to do it: (1) Find the main predicate/root. (2) Ask which word is its subject and object. (3) Attach modifiers to the word they describe, not automatically to the main verb. (4) Label each link with the relation between the dependent and its head. (5) Check that every word belongs to the tree and there is only one root.

Example: “The student reads a book” — reads is the root; student is its subject and book its object. “The” depends on “student”; “a” depends on “book”.

Correct: 0 of 50

Each level contains 10 questions. Explanations identify the correct head, explain the dependency labels, and clarify why an alternative root is incorrect.

Labeled Bracketing Lab

Represent sentence structure by placing words inside nested brackets and labeling each constituent (S, NP, VP, PP, and others).

How labeled bracketing works

Purpose: Labeled bracketing displays the hierarchical structure of a sentence using square brackets and category labels.

How to read it: Each opening bracket introduces a constituent label; its matching closing bracket marks where that constituent ends. Smaller constituents are nested inside larger ones.

Example: “The child laughed.” The sentence contains a noun phrase subject and a verb phrase predicate:

[S
  [NP [Det The] [N child]]
  [VP [V laughed]]]

Common labels: S = sentence, NP = noun phrase, VP = verb phrase, PP = prepositional phrase, Det = determiner, N = noun, V = verb, P = preposition, AdjP = adjective phrase, AdvP = adverb phrase, CP = complementiser phrase.

Identify basic sentence constituents.

Phonetics Exercises

  
A guided learning space for understanding how English speech sounds are produced, heard, described and organized.

  

   
   
   
   
   
  

  

   
Purpose of this learning area

    
These activities help you develop the knowledge and practical skills needed to describe, identify and transcribe speech sounds. Phonetics is useful for English majors because pronunciation, listening, oral communication and language analysis all depend on understanding the sound system of speech.

    
Learning outcomes
  • Explain the difference between phonetics and phonology.
  • Identify vowels and consonants using IPA symbols.
  • Describe consonants by voicing, place and manner of articulation.
  • Recognize syllable structure, stress, rhythm and intonation.
  • Interpret broad and narrow phonetic transcriptions.
  • Apply sound concepts when listening to and analyzing spoken English.

    
How to use this section
  1. Read the study guide before attempting a new topic.
  2. Explore the IPA chart and glossary when you encounter unfamiliar symbols or terms.
  3. Complete the levels in order and read the explanation after every answer.
  4. Retry a level to strengthen your understanding, not only to increase your score.

    
Important: English pronunciation varies across accents. Examples in these exercises use common broad IPA descriptions; some symbols and vowel qualities may differ by dictionary or English variety.

   

  

  

   
Study guide: the foundations of phonetics

    
1. What is phonetics?
Phonetics is the scientific study of speech sounds. It examines how sounds are produced by the vocal organs (articulatory phonetics), how sound travels through the air (acoustic phonetics), and how listeners perceive speech (auditory phonetics).
Example: When producing /p/, the two lips close, pressure builds, and the lips release the air.

    
2. Phonetics and phonology
Phonetics focuses on the physical properties of speech sounds. Phonology studies how a language organizes sounds into a system of contrasts and patterns.
Example: Phonetics describes the sound [pʰ]. Phonology considers whether /p/ contrasts with /b/ in a language.

    
3. Consonants: voicing, place and manner
Voicing asks whether the vocal folds vibrate. Place identifies where the airflow is narrowed or stopped. Manner describes how the airflow is modified.
  • /p/: voiceless bilabial stop
  • /b/: voiced bilabial stop
  • /s/: voiceless alveolar fricative
  • /m/: voiced bilabial nasal
  • /k/: voiceless velar stop

    
4. Vowels
Vowels are produced without a complete blockage of airflow in the vocal tract. They are commonly described by tongue height (high, mid, low), tongue position (front, central, back), and lip shape (rounded or unrounded). Vowel systems vary considerably across English accents.

    
5. Syllables and stress
A syllable commonly has an onset, a nucleus and an optional coda. In “cat” /kæt/, /k/ is the onset, /æ/ is the nucleus and /t/ is the coda. Stress makes a syllable more prominent through a combination of cues such as pitch, duration and intensity.

    
6. Transcription: / / and [ ]
Slashes / / usually mark phonemic transcription, which represents contrastive units. Square brackets [ ] mark phonetic transcription, which can show more detailed pronunciation. Diacritics add information such as aspiration or nasalization.

    
7. Connected speech and prosody
In connected speech, sounds may link, become more alike (assimilation), weaken (reduction), or disappear (elision). Prosody includes stress, rhythm and intonation. Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance.
